summary: A request for comments on using the ARPANET's resources for Computer Based Instruction. It describes existing standalone and centralized systems and asks the community how network resources might be applied, aiming to start a dialogue.

plainLanguage.summary: Could schools use the computer network to teach students? The author wants ideas.

subtitle: Could the ARPANET's resources help schools teach students?

tldr.problem: Computer Based Instruction (CBI) systems were being developed in isolation; the potential of the ARPANET for education was not well understood by either CBI developers or network people.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes four areas where ARPANET resources could benefit CBI: the network itself as a communication backbone, centralized data storage for lessons and management data, language processors for diverse instructional needs, and dialogue support systems for collaboration.
tldr.outcome: This early exploration of network-enabled education identified problems and opportunities that would shape distance learning and distributed systems for decades.

today: RFC 313 is a historical request for comments proposing the use of the ARPANET for education. While not a standard or specification, it represents an early vision of distance learning and network-enabled education that would become mainstream decades later.

sections.title: Computer Based Instruction and Network Resources
sections.content: The RFC explores how the ARPANET could support Computer Based Instruction (CBI), which encompasses both Computer Aided Instruction (CAI), where computers present lessons and test students, and Computer Managed Instruction (CMI), where computers manage the educational process. At the time, CBI systems were being developed independently at universities and military training centers. The RFC asks: what could the ARPANET contribute?
sections.plainLanguage: Schools were making computer teaching programs. Could they use the network to make teaching better?

sections.title: Four Ways the Network Could Help
sections.content: The RFC identifies four valuable areas: (1) The network itself as a communications backbone, allowing distributed terminals to reach CBI centers or allowing centers to be shared geographically; (2) Centralized data storage, reducing costs through economy of scale and allowing unified management data across institutions; (3) Language processors, since CBI requires text handling, logic for multiple-choice responses, simulation, and statistical processing—capabilities available from different computers on the network; (4) Dialogue support systems, letting researchers and educators collaborate in real time rather than through memos and meetings.
sections.plainLanguage: The network could carry students to teachers, store lesson materials, provide tools for making lessons, and let teachers talk to each other live.

sections.title: From Testing to Wide Adoption
sections.content: The RFC imagines practical steps: a geographically isolated school could test a major CBI center over the network before installing its own, or build up to it gradually. Existing network resources could be used to test new languages and data systems before building dedicated CBI systems. Meta-compiler techniques could allow portable CBI software across different manufacturers' hardware, reducing the cost of system development and allowing hardware choices based on cost-effectiveness rather than software constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Schools could try a teaching program on the network, then build their own when ready. The same lesson could run on different computers.
